title: Pokhara in three days: a local plan
meta_description: Three days in Pokhara planned by locals: Phewa Lake and the Peace Pagoda, Sarangkot sunrise, caves and the old bazaar, then paragliding or a short hike.
summary: Day one: Phewa Lake by boat, Tal Barahi and the World Peace Pagoda. Day two: Sarangkot sunrise, Davis Falls, Gupteshwor cave, the old bazaar and the mountain museum. Day three: paragliding, the Begnas lakes or a short walk to Australian Camp. Stay in Lakeside, go early for the mountains, and keep afternoons slow.

sections.heading: How Pokhara fits together
paras: Pokhara is Nepal's second city, but for visitors it feels like a lake town. Lakeside, the strip of hotels, cafes and shops along the east shore of Phewa Lake, is where almost everyone stays. Damside, at the south end by the dam, is quieter and has some of the best morning views of Machhapuchhre across the water. The old city, with its Newar bazaar and temples, lies a few kilometres north-east, around Bindhyabasini temple and the Bhimsen temple, and very few tourists go there.

Above the lake to the north is the ridge of Sarangkot, about 1,600 m, the classic sunrise point and the launch site for paragliders. Across the lake to the south-west, the white World Peace Pagoda stands on its own ridge. And 15 km east, Begnas and Rupa lakes sit among fish farms and rice terraces. The Seti river cuts through the whole city in a gorge so narrow and deep that you can cross it without noticing.

The mountains are the backdrop to all of it. Machhapuchhre, 6,993 m, is only about 30 km from Lakeside in a straight line, which is why it looks so huge from the shore. It is clearest in the morning, so plan anything that needs a view before 10 am.

sections.heading: Day one: the lake and the pagoda
paras: Start slowly with breakfast in Lakeside, then walk down to the boat station near the Barahi temple ghat. Hire a wooden doonga with a boatman, or paddle yourself, and cross to the island temple of Tal Barahi, a small two-tiered pagoda dedicated to the goddess Barahi, a form of Durga. On Saturdays local families queue with offerings, and the boats are busy; on a weekday it is calm.

From the island, ask your boatman to take you across to the south shore below the World Peace Pagoda. A stone path climbs through forest for about an hour. The pagoda was built by monks of the Japanese Nipponzan-Myohoji order, and its white dome and gilded Buddha statues look out over the lake, the city and the full Annapurna range. Walk down the other side toward Pardi and Damside, or go back to the boat.

In the afternoon wander Lakeside, sit in a lakeside garden with a pot of tea, and come back to the shore at sunset when the boats come in and Machhapuchhre often clears for a few minutes in pink light.

If you have energy left, walk north along the shore past the end of the main strip, where the hotels thin out, rice fields reach the water and the view of Machhapuchhre is free of rooftops. Cyclists and buffalo share the road here, and the lakeside tea stalls are cheaper than the cafes in town.

sections.heading: Day two: sunrise, caves and the old bazaar
paras: Get up at about 5 am for the 30-minute drive to Sarangkot. From the viewpoint you see Dhaulagiri in the west, the Annapurnas and Machhapuchhre in the middle, and Lamjung Himal to the east, with Phewa Lake below in the valley mist. Bring a warm layer from November to February; it is cold before the sun comes up.

After breakfast drive to the south of the city for Davis Falls, called Patale Chhango in Nepali, the underworld falls, where the outflow of Phewa Lake drops into a sinkhole and vanishes. Across the road is Gupteshwor Mahadev cave, with a Shiva lingam in its first chamber and, further in, a view of the same water falling through the rock. Both take about an hour together.

In the afternoon visit the International Mountain Museum, with displays on the great peaks, the history of mountaineering and the peoples of the Himalaya, then head to the old bazaar. Bindhyabasini temple sits on a small hill with a view of the range, and the lanes around it still have some old Newar shopfronts with carved wooden windows.

sections.heading: Day three: pick your adventure
paras: Pokhara's third day should match what you came for. For the adrenaline, tandem paragliding from Sarangkot is the most popular single activity in the city: 20 to 30 minutes in the air with a licensed pilot, landing on the lakeshore. The ZipFlyer, a long zipline from near Sarangkot, about 1.8 km long, is another option. Both are weather-dependent and best booked a day ahead.

For a taste of trekking, drive an hour to Kande and walk two hours up to Australian Camp for lunch with a full view of Machhapuchhre and the Annapurnas, then walk down via Dhampus to Phedi and drive back. You will need an ACAP permit and a licensed guide for this; check current status before you travel.
For something slow, go to Begnas Lake, rent a rowing boat, and walk the ridge to Rupa Lake. It feels like a different town: no cafes, just fish farms, paddy fields and the occasional kingfisher.

sections.heading: Where to eat and what to try
paras: Lakeside has every cuisine a traveller could want, but try at least three local things. A Thakali set, from the Thakali people of the Kali Gandaki valley, is a refined dal bhat with buckwheat or rice, gundruk, pickles and ghee; several Thakali kitchens in Lakeside and the city serve it. Fried fish from Phewa or Begnas, usually small whole fish, is a Pokhara speciality, eaten with beaten rice and chilli. And sel roti, a sweet ring of rice-flour bread, is sold in the morning in the old bazaar, especially around festivals.
For a sundowner, the lakeside gardens at the north end of Lakeside are quieter than the main strip. Bakeries open early for trekkers, so breakfast before a sunrise drive is easy to find.

If you are in Pokhara for a festival, the food changes with it. At Dashain in autumn families cook goat meat and the city empties as people go home to their villages. At Tihar, a few weeks later, houses are lit with oil lamps and children go from door to door singing deusi and bhailo songs for sweets and small coins. Ask your guide or hotel what is on during your stay.

sections.heading: Getting there and getting around
paras: Pokhara is about 200 km from Kathmandu by road, 6 to 8 hours on the Prithvi Highway by tourist bus or private car, or 25 minutes by air. Pokhara International Airport opened in January 2023 east of the city. Within Pokhara, taxis are easy to find, but agree the fare before you get in. Lakeside is flat and walkable, and bicycles and scooters can be rented.
A few practical points will make the three days smoother.

Pokhara is also the natural end of most Annapurna treks, so many travellers do their three days here after walking. If that is you, put the slow day first: a boat, a massage and a long lunch. Save Sarangkot and paragliding for when your legs have recovered.
list: Go to Sarangkot and the lakeshore early; afternoon cloud usually hides the mountains.
Wear a life jacket on boats, and ask for one for children.
Book paragliding and the ZipFlyer a day ahead in October and November.
Dress modestly and remove shoes at Tal Barahi and Bindhyabasini temples.
Carry small notes for entry fees and boat tips.

faqs.q: Is three days enough for Pokhara?
faqs.a: Yes, for the main sights. Three days gives time for Phewa Lake and the Peace Pagoda, a Sarangkot sunrise, Davis Falls, the caves, the museum and one activity like paragliding or a short hike. With a fourth or fifth day, add Begnas Lake or a two-night trek to Australian Camp and Dhampus.

faqs.q: What is the best area to stay in Pokhara?
faqs.a: Lakeside is the most convenient, with hotels, restaurants and boats on your doorstep. Damside, at the south end, is quieter and has fine morning views across the lake. For peace and space, resorts in the hills outside the city, or a lodge by Begnas Lake, are good choices if you are happy to use a car.

faqs.q: When can you see the mountains from Pokhara?
faqs.a: From October to February the mountains are usually clear in the mornings, often all day in November and December. In March and April haze builds by mid-morning. In the monsoon, June to September, the peaks are hidden most days. The best chance of a view is at dawn from Sarangkot or the lakeshore.

faqs.q: How do I get to Sarangkot for sunrise?
faqs.a: Take a taxi from Lakeside, about 30 minutes, leaving around 5 am in autumn and winter. The road goes almost to the viewpoint, with a short walk of 10 to 15 minutes to the top. You can also hike up from Lakeside in about two hours on a steep path, best done in daylight.

Pokhara is one of the most popular tandem paragliding sites in Asia, and licensed operators have a good record. Choose an established company, check that your pilot is licensed and that your travel insurance covers paragliding. Flights are cancelled in bad weather. Most flights last 20 to 30 minutes from Sarangkot to the lakeshore.

faqs.q: What food is Pokhara known for?
faqs.a: Pokhara is known for fried lake fish, Thakali dal bhat sets from the Kali Gandaki valley, and sel roti in the old bazaar. Lakeside also has many bakeries and international restaurants serving trekkers. Try a Thakali set with buckwheat dhido and gundruk at least once.

faqs.q: Can I visit the World Peace Pagoda without hiking?
faqs.a: Yes. A road reaches close to the pagoda from the south side of the lake, and a taxi from Lakeside takes about 30 minutes, followed by a short walk. The most enjoyable way, however, is by boat across Phewa and up the forest path, about an hour of climbing on stone steps.

Yes. Lakeside is flat and safe to walk, boats and caves appeal to children, and paragliding and the ZipFlyer suit older children who meet the weight limits. The mountain museum and short hikes are easy. Many hotels have family rooms, and some resorts have pools.

faqs.q: How do I get from Kathmandu to Pokhara?
faqs.a: Fly in about 25 minutes, or take a tourist bus or private car on the Prithvi Highway, about 200 km and 6 to 8 hours depending on traffic and road work. Tourist buses leave Kathmandu early in the morning. A private car lets you stop at Bandipur or the Manakamana cable car on the way.
